Everything is K-shaped , so your plans must be too
The mediocre and low quality are not judged negatively - just ignored

Recently a student pinged me and asked me if University X is considered reputed.I don't want to name the university here because that will detour the conversation but its definitely in the top 30 but not top 10. I pressed them some more and understood how they were approaching this concern or what exactly their pre-conditioning was. The problem is students are assuming recruiters/EMs/founders are looking at a resume and making a determination that a university is reputed - but in reality that doesn't happen at all!

If a decision maker sees an average university on your resume their perception is not that its bad, its just ignored thats all. And the problem is the quality of 'average' has gotten wide enough that its nearly everything now except the very very top.

Even if your resume said you went to Stanford and thats about it - atleast you'd summon some reaction in the readers eye . If they are to talk about you they'd say he's a stanford grad but thats it? But if you have stanford and 3 more things now you're in the category where you can Wow them or atleast capture some attention space.

The point is no one is negatively or harshly judging your credentials and skills, they are simply ignoring it . This is actually worse because its a non-reaction. A number of things have made it like this now but very briefly AI makes expectations much higher and attention was always a premium.

The takeaway here is that you shouldn't be concerned too much about the reputation of your markers (University, Grades, YOE, Skills) , you should be asking if you can capture attention and Wow the reader. A T10 admit/degree is one thing that can help but even that cannot be the only thing anymore. So a T30 admit/degree that has nothing else going for it but the same old YOE, Skills will be yawned over.

Everything is K-shaped now

The broader pattern here is the K-shapedness of everything now. Or the middle is thinning out. For years you may have heard the middle class is thinning out but this phenomenon is happening everywhere now.

Careers are K-shaped especially in software - either you're working at Foundation labs with a sure path to being a millionaire or its risk of layoffs - there's no middle

Funding and VC is K-shaped - most VCs want to pile on into OpenAI / Anthropic instead of taking a bet on some random new thing - there is no middle

The S&P 500 and index funds are clearly K shaped - a handful of individual companies control the index and the rest are at 0 or even negative - there is no middle

In this scenario you must ask yourself what does a K-shaped strategy for you look like. If you target acquiring mediocre admits/degrees you're intentionally placing yourself in the middle zone - that is melting away. A K-shaped strategy would either optimize for all the hits or not do grad school at all. A K-shaped strategy also shows up in how many applications you send out - either send out 15+ or better to just not apply.

K-shapedness means everyone is shooting for the fences and showing up with all the ammo and guns they have for the game , or they are at home and have decided to not even play. Those are the reasonable strategies left and the mediocre strategy that looks reasonable actually ends up being bad because it targets an opportunity space that is in the middle and actively reducing.

Treat Risk as a variable not an externality

Most students treat Risk as an externality - a thing that happens to them

A student asking ROI of sending out 5 applications vs 10 vs 20 is clearly treating Risk as a variable they control but a student asking what is the ROI of Univ X is treating Risk as an externality.

Risk does exist as an externality but Risk is also a variable you have at your disposal. If the middle is thinning out and the only options are to shoot for the fences or not play , then you have to actively take Risk and roll the dice for the fences.

Safe harbors

But its not for everyone, so what are the safe harbors? In terms of careers there are some human needs that will have continuity despite AI - stuff like childcare, services (the hospitality / entertainment / handyman trades stuff , not the IT services), healthcare etc . Maybe you wont accrue massive wealth (doctors will) but such jobs will have a continuity to them because there is a direct human dependence to them. Thats a good way to identify these jobs.

Software unfortunately is in the process of thinning out and looking K-shaped. If mass workforce does exist for software the lower end of it would more so be janitorial work for the AIs while the other extreme would be a few top engineers that build the AIs.

Pursuing fields that are still unclear (robotics and hardware/ cv or vision / computational biology) or pursuing the pure engineering & sciences and aiming to be the very best at it ( cs theory , math, statistics ) is a Risk variable that can pay off. It pays off because the immediate outcome is unclear but in the future there will always be a demand for leading edge and from-first-principle engineers & scientists. The obvious path here is a phd and committing to it.

How do recent CPT interpretation changes affect the ROI of a US MSCS degree for international students?
Reposting because the original post was removed.

My interpretation of the current situation is as follows:

• If CPT is no longer broadly available and is restricted to programs where it is a required part of the curriculum, many students in traditional 2-year MS programs effectively lose access to summer internships.

• No internships means a significantly lower to ~0 ROI for many international students.

• Internships were never a guarantee of employment, but they were one of the few ways to demonstrate value to US employers, build local experience, and convert into full-time opportunities.

• Nobody is owed an internship or a job. However, there is a difference between failing in an open competition and not being allowed to enter the competition in the first place. If internship pathways disappear, many students lose their primary opportunity to prove themselves. Without proof no one sponsors.

• Universities were happy to collect international tuition. Many students accepted those costs because they believed they would at least have an opportunity to compete in the labor market. That assumption is now being challenged. No free labor market.

• Pre-completion OPT is often presented as an alternative, but it comes with tradeoffs. It consumes OPT time, may require premium processing, and creates additional uncertainty and cost. Students should budget for that reality. Please pay for the PP and get your EAD. Do not compromise here. Include PP as part of your funds.

• Internships historically helped international students gain the US experience that many recruiters and hiring managers ask for. Without that bridge, how are employers expected to evaluate candidates whose previous experience was obtained outside the US?

• I find it strange that someone can have several years of experience at a top company outside the US, yet suddenly be treated as if they have no relevant experience when applying from within the US. I am interested in hearing recruiters' and hiring managers' views on this.

• Prospective students should carefully evaluate whether a program has mandatory co-op or internship requirements. If employment is one of your primary goals, this may become an important factor in university selection. Select the one with co-op if you depend on job post graduation. No questions asked.

• Students taking significant loans should evaluate programs assuming a conservative outcome. Assume the internship does not happen. Assume the job offer does not happen. Then decide whether the financial risk still makes sense.

• If these CPT interpretations remain in place, I do not expect the situation to improve quickly unless universities successfully challenge them or adapt their programs.

• The traditional value proposition for many international students was not just the education itself, but also the opportunity to compete in the US labor market. If the avenues for gaining experience are reduced, the economics of that decision change materially. In my opinion it is 0.

• For students considering a US degree today, it may be worth evaluating alternative countries, alternative pathways, or a plan that assumes returning home after graduation.

My view is simple: nobody owes international students internships or jobs. But students should have a realistic understanding of the risks before committing substantial time, money, and family resources to a degree. The removal of CPT limits your time to compete 24/7 which was the greatest asset for an intl student.

I am making this post since it was requested deep in a debate thread here. Linking my response promising it

90% of you should drop plans for MS.

First it was requested that I say this out loud "as an owner of this forum ". 90% of you should drop plans to come to USA for MS. The remainder 10% should know that immigration uncertainty is high and bar for getting hired is high as well. I'll expand on this below

Immigration uncertainty and misinformation

First you should make sure you have accurate news and information. Immigration uncertainty being high means there's a lot of new laws and bills and other ordinances in play and in the air right now. This doesn't mean that OPT/H1B is dead. It just means its in a state where it could be dead but has to be played out. Thats the uncertainty you have to contend with. It might be that nothing happens - the 100K H1B was shot down . Its not a coincidence that the same 100K amount showed up but now upstream at the OPT door. Will it get shot down too ? My personal opinion is yes it will but I'm not in the white house neither a person of influence. This is the uncertainty. You shouldn't have to believe me you just need to accept that the current times we are in requires you to live with the fact that immigration status remains unclear everyday . The minute something is decided its not uncertain or unclear. it will become abundantly clear that OPT is dead in its tracks, then its not uncertain anymore.

The supply dynamics of international students, AI and Meat Proxies

Since 2020 the number of Indian students coming into USA every year has sharply increased. Not marginally but sharply. One controversial statement here is that the average skill level (for something like CS engineering stuff) of a population drops when population size increases.

The other fact is that upto 2020 or so getting hired as a full stack engineer or similar - the largest population of labor that was needed for tech - was relatively easy and in high demand . The work was getting standardized and the education was too. The demand existed as well. In this period starting with low/basic skills and quickly upskilling was easy. This vanished overnight with AI

Now we have "meat proxies" - meat proxy is a new slang, maybe a new slur, showing up in SF/SV. A meat proxy is a human engineer who sits between their team and claude-code/codex. They simply relay what the AI tells them. If you're a meat proxy your career is dead. The foundation labs and big tech know this so interviews have gotten harder now in 2026. They want people who can think and communicate critically. The LC skills from 2020 will not be enough in 2026 you'll be grilled a lot harder since no one wants to hire a meat proxy in their team given AI bills are also going to shoot up anytime soon.

When I put all this together here is what I see:
- immigration getting uncertain makes everyone anxious
- hiring bar is up
- the supply of low/avg skill engs in the system is high because universities liberally admit many and make up new random programs ad-hoc. they are losing revenue - thats another story - but they have to make it up somehow.

And what happens in a public anon community like this is you have students claiming no one is hiring. The fact of the matter is hiring is still on. H1B 100K is not a thing and can be sponsored, big tech, foundation labs and startups want very high skill and talented engs who are not meat proxies and filing h1b is not some new thing for them it has been standard process for more than 25 years.

When you read an anon student claiming no one is hiring because of sponsorship you need to ask a few questions:
- is it because this person cannot clear a high bar interview which is common place now
- is it because they are anxious about immigration uncertainty and maybe they are an experienced engineer also in the market. or what is commonly called gatekeeping.

The data of H1B issuances is public you can look up who is filing new H1Bs and job descriptions will clearly state if they cannot sponsor visas . My ex-employer has a new grad position open with no statement that sponsorship will not be provided. What does this mean? They want you to apply and see if you can match their bar.

If you can match the bar of new AI companies and you can deal with uncertainty of Visas sure take your shot. Just know the risk.

If you are looking to crack easy interviews or find an easy low stress job, those days are over. I've previously stated that anyone coming to USA and optimizing for careers should aggressively try to get to SV/SF and aim for an exponential growth career.

A lot of students want low stress , 'stable' jobs in middle-of-nowhere america , doing IT stuff, or full stack REST CRUD development. Those days are shockingly behind us and in an anonymous forum like this its not clear if you're talking to someone trying to optimize that path or actually appearing for an OpenAI interview tomorrow who will file his H1B if he meets their bar
